questions.stem: Pemulwuy, a Bidjigal man, is remembered in Australian history for:
options: leading armed resistance around Sydney and Parramatta until his death in 1802
negotiating the first written treaty between Aboriginal people and the Sydney colony
guiding the first colonial expedition across the Blue Mountains in 1813
petitioning Governor Macquarie for land beside the Parramatta Native Institution
questions.explanation: From about 1790 Pemulwuy led raids on farms and fought colonial parties around Sydney, Parramatta and the Hawkesbury until he was shot in 1802. No treaty was made in the Sydney colony; the absence of any treaty is a lasting feature of Australian colonisation.

questions.stem: In 1824 Governor Brisbane declared martial law in the district west of the Blue Mountains. This was a response to:
options: a convict uprising among assigned servants on the Bathurst sheep stations
riots by miners on the Bathurst goldfields against the licence fee
a bushranging campaign by escaped convicts along the western road
Wiradjuri resistance to pastoral expansion around Bathurst
questions.explanation: As settlers and their stock spread over Wiradjuri Country, Wiradjuri people led by Windradyne fought back, and martial law was declared in August 1824. Gold was not found near Bathurst until 1851, so a goldfields riot is decades too early.

questions.stem: The Myall Creek massacre of 1838 stands out in the history of the New South Wales frontier because:
options: the killings were carried out by Native Police acting on the governor's orders
seven colonists were hanged, a rare punishment for frontier killings
it was the last recorded killing of Aboriginal people on the New South Wales frontier
the colonial government apologised and granted land to the Wirrayaraay survivors
questions.explanation: Stockmen murdered Wirrayaraay women, children and old men in June 1838. After an acquittal at the first trial, seven men were retried, convicted and hanged in December 1838. Killings did not stop; many colonists resented the verdict and violence on the frontier continued, often more secretly.

questions.stem: In 1830 Lieutenant-Governor Arthur organised the 'Black Line' across settled Van Diemen's Land. What was the outcome?
options: It ended the Black War by driving every Aboriginal clan onto the Tasman Peninsula
It led to a treaty signed by Arthur and the leaders of the eastern Tasmanian nations
It was abandoned when the Colonial Office ordered Arthur to end martial law at once
It captured only two people and was seen as a costly failure
questions.explanation: More than 2,000 soldiers, settlers and convicts swept across the island for weeks but caught only two people. The Black War ended not through the Line but through George Augustus Robinson's later missions, after which survivors were exiled to Wybalenna on Flinders Island.

questions.stem: Jandamarra, a Bunuba man, is significant in the history of the frontier because he:
options: led armed resistance to police and pastoralists in the Kimberley from 1894 to 1897
led the walk-off of Aboriginal stockmen from Wave Hill station over wages
was the first Aboriginal man elected to a colonial parliament in Western Australia
negotiated a permanent reserve for the Bunuba with the Western Australian government
questions.explanation: Jandamarra had worked as a police tracker but turned against the police in 1894 and led a guerrilla campaign in the Kimberley ranges until he was killed in 1897. The Wave Hill walk-off was made by Gurindji workers in 1966, long after this period.

questions.stem: In 1842 Tunnerminnerwait and Maulboyheenner, two Aboriginal men from Van Diemen's Land, were hanged in Melbourne after attacks in the Western Port district. Historians now often present them as:
options: resistance fighters, executed as colonial law was turned on Aboriginal resistance
bushrangers working with escaped convicts, whose crimes had no link to dispossession
the leaders of a treaty delegation, whose execution ended negotiations with the Kulin
Native Police troopers, punished for killing settlers while on duty in Gippsland
questions.explanation: The two men had come to Port Phillip with George Augustus Robinson and later carried out armed attacks that killed two whalers. Their public execution, the first in Melbourne, is now commemorated as part of the story of Aboriginal resistance rather than treated as simple crime.

questions.stem: From the 1870s William Barak and other Coranderrk residents walked to Melbourne to put their case to the government. They were seeking:
options: the closure of Coranderrk and a move to the Lake Tyers mission
to keep Coranderrk as their home and a say in how it was run
permission to leave the reserve and take up selections in Gippsland
the removal of all residents of mixed descent from the station
questions.explanation: Coranderrk residents used petitions, deputations and letters to newspapers to resist the Board for the Protection of Aborigines' plans to close or sell the station and to object to managers imposed on them. Their campaign helped bring about the 1881 inquiry into Coranderrk.

questions.stem: In 'The Other Side of the Frontier' (1981), Henry Reynolds argued that:
options: Aboriginal people mostly welcomed pastoral settlement and only rarely fought back
conflict was confined to the first years of settlement around Sydney Cove
Aboriginal resistance was widespread and could be traced in colonial records
frontier violence had been greatly exaggerated by missionaries and humanitarian reformers
questions.explanation: Reynolds used settler diaries, newspapers and official records to reconstruct how Aboriginal people saw and resisted colonisation across the continent. The view that violence was exaggerated belongs to later critics such as Keith Windschuttle, part of the so-called history wars.

questions.stem: In his 1968 Boyer Lectures the anthropologist W.E.H. Stanner described a 'great Australian silence'. He meant that:
options: settlers had kept no written records of their conflicts with Aboriginal people
general histories had largely left Aboriginal people out of the national story
Aboriginal people had refused to speak to colonial officials about the loss of their land
colonial governments had censored newspaper reports of violence on the frontier
questions.explanation: Stanner argued that a 'cult of forgetfulness' meant general histories hardly mentioned Aboriginal people after the first chapters. Settlers did leave many records of conflict, which is how historians such as Reynolds later recovered the history.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the extent of change for Aboriginal people as colonial democracy grew between 1856 and 1901?
options: Settler democracy widened while protection laws tightened control of Aboriginal people
Aboriginal men lost the vote in every colony when responsible government was granted
Federation transferred control of Aboriginal affairs from the states to the Commonwealth
Aboriginal people gained secure title to reserves as a result of manhood suffrage
questions.explanation: In several colonies Aboriginal men technically gained the vote under manhood suffrage, but protection boards, reserves and the loss of land meant growing control over their lives. The Constitution left Aboriginal affairs with the states, so Federation did not transfer control to the Commonwealth.

questions.stem: The Australian Colonies Government Act 1850, passed by the British Parliament, is significant for Victoria because it:
options: separated the Port Phillip District from New South Wales as Victoria
gave Victoria responsible government with two fully elected houses of parliament
introduced manhood suffrage for the first Victorian Legislative Council
joined the Port Phillip District and Van Diemen's Land into a single colony
questions.explanation: Port Phillip settlers had long agitated for separation from distant Sydney, and the Act created Victoria, which began on 1 July 1851. Its first Legislative Council was partly elected on a property franchise; responsible government came only in 1855.

questions.stem: Responsible government, granted to most eastern colonies in the mid-1850s, meant that:
options: all adult men and women could vote for both houses of parliament
the ministry had to keep the confidence of the elected lower house
the governor chose all ministers from among the Legislative Council
Britain stopped appointing governors to the self-governing colonies
questions.explanation: Under responsible government, ministers sat in parliament and governed only while they had the support of the elected Legislative Assembly, as in Britain. Governors were still appointed from London, and women did not yet vote.

questions.stem: In 1856 Victoria and South Australia became among the first places in the world to use the secret ballot. Reformers wanted it because it:
options: allowed women to vote without their husbands knowing their choice
made counting faster in large country electorates far from towns
limited voting to men who could read and write the candidates' names
shielded voters from pressure by employers and landlords
questions.explanation: Open voting let powerful men see how their workers and tenants voted. The secret ballot, a Chartist demand, became known as the 'Australian ballot'. Women did not vote in colonial elections until the 1890s and later.

questions.stem: By the 1860s most Victorian men could vote for the Legislative Assembly, yet radicals still argued that democracy was incomplete. Their main target was:
options: a law barring goldfields miners from voting for the Legislative Assembly
a property-franchise Legislative Council able to block Assembly bills
the Governor's power to appoint a Premier from outside the elected parliament
the lack of a secret ballot in Legislative Assembly elections in country areas
questions.explanation: Victoria's Legislative Council, chosen by men of property, rejected Assembly measures such as the 1865 tariff and payment of members, causing constitutional crises in the 1860s and 1870s. Miners had gained the vote through the Miner's Right and then manhood suffrage in 1857.

questions.stem: Which grievance did miners at Ballarat raise in the months before the Eureka Stockade?
options: the call-up of miners into a colonial militia for service in the Crimean War
the monthly licence fee, enforced by armed 'digger hunts'
a new duty on all gold exported to Britain, imposed by Governor Hotham that year
the closure of the Ballarat alluvial diggings to individual miners and small parties
questions.explanation: Miners resented paying a licence fee regardless of success and the often brutal licence hunts by police. An export duty on gold was introduced after Eureka as part of the reforms that replaced the licence.

questions.stem: The Ballarat Reform League's charter of November 1854 demanded:
options: the exclusion of all Chinese miners from the Ballarat and Bendigo goldfields
the replacement of the Legislative Council by elected miners' courts
manhood suffrage, payment of members and no property test for members
an independent Victorian republic with no allegiance to the British Crown
questions.explanation: The charter called for political rights that echoed the People's Charter, as well as the abolition of the licence fee and the Gold Commission. It said the League did not seek immediate separation from Britain.

questions.stem: Several Ballarat Reform League demands closely followed the British People's Charter of 1838. This suggests that:
options: goldfields protest was mainly a campaign for Irish independence
radical ideas travelled with British migrants into goldfields protest
the League was directed by agents of the Chartist leadership in London
the Chartists in Britain had already won these reforms before 1854
questions.explanation: Many diggers had seen or taken part in Chartism in Britain and carried its demands, such as manhood suffrage and payment of members, to Victoria. Britain did not grant most of the Charter's points until decades later.

questions.stem: In 1855 thirteen men were tried for high treason after the Eureka Stockade. The result was that:
options: all were hanged at the Melbourne Gaol
all were transported to Norfolk Island
only Peter Lalor was convicted and jailed
all were acquitted by Melbourne juries
questions.explanation: Juries refused to convict, a sign of public sympathy for the miners. Peter Lalor was not among those tried; he escaped capture, was wounded and later entered parliament.

questions.stem: Which reform followed the Goldfields Commission of Enquiry after Eureka?
options: Victoria gave the vote to women living on the goldfields
Gold mining was restricted to companies holding Crown leases
The licence became a cheaper Miner's Right that carried a vote
The goldfields police were placed under the control of elected miners
questions.explanation: The Commission recommended abolishing the licence. A Miner's Right costing one pound a year and an export duty on gold replaced it, and holders of a Miner's Right gained the vote. Victorian women did not gain the state vote until 1908.

questions.stem: Historians debate whether Eureka was a turning point for Australian democracy. Which evidence most supports the view that it was?
options: Many of the rebels were foreign-born, including Americans, Italians and Germans
Within three years Victoria had manhood suffrage, the secret ballot and Lalor in parliament
South Australia introduced similar democratic reforms in 1856 without any armed rebellion
The Stockade was overrun by soldiers and police in a dawn attack lasting a short time
questions.explanation: Rapid reform after Eureka supports the turning-point view. South Australia's reforms, achieved peacefully, point the other way: democracy was coming in the colonies with or without the rebellion. The speed of the defeat and the rebels' origins do not show democratic change.

questions.stem: In the 1840s squatters in New South Wales pressed the British government for:
options: a land tax on large estates to fund railways to the interior
secure long leases over their runs and the right to buy them
the abolition of convict transportation to New South Wales
small farms for ex-convicts on the edges of the pastoral runs
questions.explanation: Squatters had occupied huge areas without title and wanted security. The Orders in Council of 1847 gave them long leases with a pre-emptive right to buy. Many squatters wanted cheap convict labour, so the anti-transportation movement drew more support from towns.

questions.stem: Free selection laws, such as the New South Wales Robertson Land Acts of 1861, aimed to:
options: set aside land for Aboriginal people beside every pastoral station in the colony
sell Crown land only by public auction to raise revenue for the colony
let small farmers select Crown land, even on squatters' runs, before survey
grant squatters freehold title to their entire runs at a nominal price per acre
questions.explanation: The cry to 'unlock the lands' reflected democratic hopes that ordinary families could farm their own land. Victoria passed similar Acts in the 1860s. The laws threatened squatters, who held most of the good land on lease.

questions.stem: Many selection laws failed to create the large class of small farmers reformers hoped for. Which practice by squatters most explains this?
options: Hiring selectors as shepherds so that they had no time to clear and farm their blocks
Dummying: agents selecting key land, such as water frontages, for the squatter
Refusing to sell wool through any cooperative that selectors had formed in the district
Persuading the colonial upper houses to repeal the selection laws soon after they passed
questions.explanation: Squatters used dummies and other tactics to secure the best land and water, leaving selectors with poorer blocks. Small block sizes, drought and lack of capital also hurt selectors. The laws were amended over time, not simply repealed.

questions.stem: In 1856 Melbourne stonemasons won an eight-hour working day. Their success is significant because:
options: it was among the first organised workers' gains of its kind anywhere in the world
it was granted by an Act of the Victorian parliament covering all workers in the colony
it followed a general strike that shut Melbourne's port for several months
it was extended at once to women working in Melbourne's clothing factories
questions.explanation: After stonemasons marched to Parliament House on 21 April 1856, building employers agreed to the shorter day. It was won by industrial action and agreement, not by legislation, and it spread only gradually to other trades.

questions.stem: 'New Unionism' in the 1880s differed from the older craft unions mainly because it:
options: admitted only skilled tradesmen who had served a formal apprenticeship
rejected strikes and relied instead on sickness and funeral benefits
was set up by employers to settle disputes without industrial action
enrolled unskilled and semi-skilled workers such as shearers
questions.explanation: Unions such as William Spence's Amalgamated Shearers' Union recruited mass memberships across whole industries and were more willing to strike and to take political action. The craft unions had been small, skilled and cautious.

questions.stem: In the Maritime Strike of 1890 and the shearers' strikes of 1891, the central issue was:
options: employers' 'freedom of contract' to hire non-union labour against union recognition
the level of the federal basic wage set by the Arbitration Court for pastoral workers
the use of Pacific Islander labour on Queensland's coastal sugar plantations
the eight-hour day for wharf labourers on the Sydney and Melbourne docks
questions.explanation: Employers insisted on the right to employ whom they chose, including non-unionists, while unions demanded closed shops and recognition. There was no federal basic wage until after Federation, so that issue is anachronistic.

questions.stem: The Tree of Knowledge at Barcaldine in Queensland is associated with:
options: the declaration of the results of the 1899 federal referendum
the first meeting of the Australian Women's Suffrage Society
the 1891 shearers' strike and the origins of the Labor Party
the founding meeting of the Ballarat Reform League in 1854
questions.explanation: Striking shearers met under the tree at their camp in 1891. Their defeat and the jailing of strike leaders pushed Queensland unionists towards forming a political party. The Ballarat Reform League met at Bakery Hill in Victoria.

questions.stem: After the defeat of the great strikes of 1890–91, many unionists concluded that they should:
options: merge with employers' associations to prevent future disputes
elect their own representatives to parliament to change the laws
abandon politics entirely and rely on general strikes alone
support free trade, which they believed would raise wages
questions.explanation: Employers had used colonial governments, police and conspiracy laws against strikers, so unions turned to politics. Labor parties formed in several colonies, and in New South Wales Labor won 35 seats at the 1891 election.

questions.stem: Anderson Dawson's government in Queensland in December 1899 is remembered because it:
options: gave Queensland women the vote for the Legislative Assembly
ended the recruitment of Pacific Islander labour for Queensland
was the world's first Labor government, lasting about a week
set up the first court of conciliation and arbitration in Australia
questions.explanation: Dawson's minority ministry was quickly defeated in parliament, but it showed that Labor could form a government. Queensland women gained the state vote in 1905, and Pacific Islander labour was ended by Commonwealth law after 1901.

questions.stem: In 1894 South Australia became the first Australian colony to give women the vote. It also gave them:
options: equal pay in the public service
the right to own property after marriage
the right to stand for parliament
the right to serve on juries
questions.explanation: South Australia's 1894 Act let women vote and stand for parliament, a world first for the right to stand. Married women's property laws had already been passed separately in the colonies, and jury service and equal pay came much later.

questions.stem: Members of the Woman's Christian Temperance Union campaigned strongly for women's suffrage in the colonies mainly because they believed that:
options: women's suffrage would bring federation of the colonies about more quickly
the vote should be limited to women who did not drink alcohol themselves
women voters would help win temperance laws to protect families
women should replace men as the majority of members in colonial parliaments
questions.explanation: The WCTU saw the vote as a means to moral and social reform, especially temperance laws to protect women and children from the effects of drink. It was one of the largest women's organisations in the suffrage campaigns.

questions.stem: The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 was a major advance for many women but a backward step for others because it:
options: gave women the federal vote but not the right to stand for parliament
excluded most Aboriginal people and other non-Europeans from voting
took the vote away from women in South Australia and Western Australia
gave the federal vote only to married women who owned property
questions.explanation: The Act gave adult women the vote and the right to stand in federal elections, but excluded 'aboriginal natives' of Australia, Asia, Africa and the Pacific Islands other than New Zealand. Section 41 was meant to protect those already on state rolls, but it was applied narrowly.

questions.stem: In 1903 Vida Goldstein stood for the Senate in Victoria. She was able to stand because:
options: the Labor Party had endorsed her after adopting female suffrage as its main policy
federal law let women stand, though Victorian women lacked the state vote
Victoria had given women the vote and the right to stand in 1894, before any other colony
the first Senate was appointed, and she was nominated to it by the Governor-General
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth Franchise Act 1902 allowed women to stand federally, and Goldstein was one of four women candidates in 1903, standing as an independent. Victoria was the last state to give women the vote, in 1908; South Australia was first in 1894.

questions.stem: Before Federation, Victoria and New South Wales took opposite positions on trade policy. Which pairing is accurate?
options: Victoria favoured free trade under Deakin; New South Wales was protectionist, backed by the Sydney Morning Herald
Both colonies were protectionist until 1890, when New South Wales switched to free trade after the Maritime Strike
Both colonies favoured free trade until Federation, when the first Commonwealth parliament introduced tariffs
Victoria was protectionist, backed by David Syme's Age; New South Wales favoured free trade under Parkes and Reid
questions.explanation: Victoria built up tariffs from the 1860s to shelter local industry and jobs, while New South Wales, relying on wool exports and Sydney's port, mostly favoured free trade. The issue divided the first federal parliament into Protectionists and Free Traders.

questions.stem: Under Alfred Deakin's 'New Protection', manufacturers would benefit from tariff protection only if they:
options: sold their goods at prices set by the Senate
gave the Commonwealth half of their shares
paid their workers 'fair and reasonable' wages
exported most of their output to Britain
questions.explanation: New Protection linked tariffs to wages, so that workers shared the benefit of protection. The Excise Tariff (Agricultural Machinery) Act 1906 put this into effect, leading to the Harvester case. The High Court struck down that Act in 1908, but the wage principle survived.

questions.stem: French observers around 1900 described Australia and New Zealand as a 'social laboratory' because they:
options: were used by Britain to trial new kinds of prisons and convict discipline
had no political parties, so experts rather than politicians made policy
tried out reforms such as women's votes, arbitration and old-age pensions
used government experimental farms to test new crops for dry inland conditions
questions.explanation: Visitors saw state experiments in democracy and welfare that were ahead of most of the world. Albert Métin called the result 'socialism without doctrines'. Political parties, including Labor, were in fact central to these reforms.

questions.stem: In his 1889 Tenterfield Oration, Henry Parkes argued that:
options: the colonies should become a republic independent of the British Empire
New South Wales should adopt Victoria's protective tariff before federating
federation should wait until women had the vote in every colony
the colonies' defence needs required a federal government and parliament
questions.explanation: Parkes cited a British military report that recommended a united defence force, and called for a convention to draft a federal constitution. He remained a free trader and a strong supporter of the British connection.

questions.stem: The Corowa Conference of 1893 revived the stalled federation movement with John Quick's proposal that:
options: New South Wales and Victoria federate first and invite the other colonies to join later
convention delegates be elected by the people and the result put to referendums
the 1891 draft constitution be adopted by the colonial premiers without further debate
the British parliament draft a constitution and impose it on all the colonies
questions.explanation: Quick's plan made federation a popular movement rather than a matter for politicians. It was adopted by the premiers and led to the elected Federal Convention of 1897–98 and the referendums of 1898–1900.

questions.stem: At the 1898 referendum a majority of New South Wales voters supported the draft constitution, but it still failed there because:
options: the Yes vote fell short of the minimum set by the New South Wales parliament
Queensland voted No on the same day, which gave it a veto over the other colonies
the votes of women were counted separately and a majority of them voted No
the British government announced it would not accept a federal constitution
questions.explanation: The New South Wales parliament required at least 80,000 Yes votes, and the Yes total fell short. After the premiers agreed amendments in 1899, a second referendum passed. Queensland did not vote in 1898.

questions.stem: Smaller colonies such as Tasmania insisted on one feature of the Constitution to protect their interests against New South Wales and Victoria. It was:
options: a veto for any single state over a constitutional referendum
equal representation of each original state in the Senate
a High Court bench with one judge drawn from each state
an equal number of House of Representatives seats per state
questions.explanation: Each original state has the same number of senators regardless of population, while House seats are shared by population. A referendum needs a national majority and a majority of states, not unanimity.

questions.stem: The Constitution combined British and American models. Which feature came mainly from the American model?
options: A federal system, with a Senate representing the states
A ministry responsible to the House of Representatives
A Governor-General representing the monarch
Government based largely on unwritten conventions
questions.explanation: Federalism and a states' house were borrowed from the United States. Responsible government and the Crown came from the British tradition, which is why the system is sometimes called the 'Washminster' model.

questions.stem: Section 51(xxxv) of the Constitution gave the Commonwealth power over conciliation and arbitration for disputes extending beyond one state. Its importance for workers was that:
options: it transferred all state factory and shops laws to the Commonwealth parliament
it gave unions the right to nominate judges to the High Court
it allowed a federal court to settle such disputes by making binding awards
it wrote a guaranteed minimum wage into the text of the Constitution itself
questions.explanation: Using this power, the Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1904 created the Commonwealth Court of Conciliation and Arbitration. Wages were not fixed in the Constitution; they were set by the court's awards, beginning with Harvester.

questions.stem: In the 1907 Harvester Judgement, Justice H.B. Higgins based a 'fair and reasonable' wage mainly on:
options: the market rate for labour set by the supply of and demand for workers
the needs of an unskilled labourer supporting a wife and about three children
the profits that H.V. McKay's harvester company could afford to share with workers
the wages paid to skilled tradesmen in British factories making similar machines
questions.explanation: Higgins asked what an unskilled man needed to live as 'a human being in a civilised community' with a family, and set 7 shillings a day. He rejected the employer's capacity to pay and the market rate as the test.

questions.stem: Harvester set a 'family wage' for men. How did this principle affect most women workers?
options: they were barred from all factory work covered by federal awards until after the First World War
employers were required to pay them a separate weekly allowance for each child in their care
their wages were set well below the male rate, as they were assumed not to support families
they were guaranteed the same basic wage as men from 1907 under the Commonwealth court's awards
questions.explanation: Because the basic wage assumed a male breadwinner, later decisions such as the 1912 Fruit Pickers case set lower rates for women in most jobs. This built gender inequality into the wage system for decades, a continuity alongside the change Harvester brought for men.
